interview_metadata.name: James Lee
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised around Paso Robles, so my life has always had vineyards, dry hills, farmers markets, and weekend events in the background. My parents are pretty practical people, and growing up they pushed me to help out, show up on time, and not act like I was too good for regular work. As a kid I was social, probably a little too talkative in class, but I was also the person organizing pickup games or trying to get friends to come to some town festival. In high school I got into volleyball, hiking, photography, and later improv, which gave me a place to be outgoing without feeling like I was just goofing off. After graduating, I went to community college in San Luis Obispo County and took general education and some hospitality and business-type classes, but I have not finished a degree yet. I worked part time in a local cafe for a while, and that taught me customer service, timing, and how much personality matters when people are visiting wine country. Lately I have been trying to turn all that into a real direction: winery events, tourism, social media, maybe eventually my own small experience company. Relationship-wise, I have never been married and do not have kids; most of my life right now is family, close friends, volleyball people, the improv group, and trying to figure out how to become more independent without rushing into a bad job.

follow_ups.question: When you picture childhood in Paso Robles, what scenes come back first?
follow_ups.response: Mostly hot afternoons, golden hills, driving past vineyards, and doing family errands that somehow ended at a community event or farmers market. I remember being around adults who knew each other through schools, tasting rooms, youth sports, or volunteer stuff, so the town felt connected.

follow_ups.question: Who were the main people shaping you growing up?
follow_ups.response: My parents for sure, plus a couple teachers who let me be energetic without shutting me down. Coaches mattered too because volleyball and team sports taught me how to be loud in a useful way instead of just taking up space.

follow_ups.question: What feels unfinished in your life story right now?
follow_ups.response: The work part. I know the direction I want, but I am still between school, odd event help, and applying for entry-level hospitality or social media jobs.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The main crossroads was after high school. I had friends leaving for four-year colleges, and part of me wanted that clean movie version of moving away and reinventing myself. But I was not sure what I wanted to study, and money was real, so I stayed local and enrolled in community college instead. At first I felt like I had failed to launch, especially when people posted dorm pictures and football games online. Then I started helping with local events, doing cafe work, taking photos for friends, and volunteering at the community garden, and I realized the thing I liked was not escaping Paso but learning how to make this place interesting for visitors and locals. That changed how I saw myself. I stopped thinking of hospitality as just serving people and started seeing it as building experiences.

follow_ups.question: Was there one event that made that click for you?
follow_ups.response: A small harvest weekend event at a winery. I was helping with check-in and photos, and I noticed I liked the whole rhythm: guests arriving, music, food timing, people asking about the vineyard, getting the Instagram posts up.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to while making that decision?
follow_ups.response: My parents, a counselor at community college, and my friend Mateo, who is very blunt. Mateo basically said, 'You light up doing events, so stop pretending you want a random major.'

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was half choice and half just following what was already happening. I consciously chose not to rush into debt for a school plan I did not believe in, but the hospitality direction came from saying yes to events and realizing I kept wanting more of that work.

follow_ups.question: Did that choice feel confident at the time?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I acted more confident than I felt, but inside I was comparing myself to friends who seemed more settled.

follow_ups.question: What made you stick with it?
follow_ups.response: Every time I helped with an event, I got real feedback from people, and that felt more convincing than just thinking about it.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, a stronger bridge from community college into local wineries or tourism offices would have helped. I knew people informally, but a real internship pipeline or mentor program would have made the path feel less random.

follow_ups.question: What kind of mentor would have been useful?
follow_ups.response: Someone running events at a winery who could show me the boring parts too, like budgets, permits, vendor contracts, and not just the fun guest-facing part.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever ask for that help?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not enough. I procrastinate on formal emails and applications, which is honestly one of my bad habits.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now, and I do not have children. My parents are the most important family in my daily life because I am living at home while I figure out work and save money. My mom is the steady planner in the family; she keeps track of appointments, birthdays, bills, and all the stuff I tend to put off. My dad is quieter and more hands-on, the kind of person who would rather fix something than talk for an hour about feelings, but he shows up. I also have a younger sister, Emily, who is still in high school, and we get along better now than we did when we were younger. We tease each other, but I drive her sometimes and help her with photo stuff for school projects. My extended family is mostly elsewhere in California, so we are not constantly together, but holidays and graduations still matter.

follow_ups.question: What does time with your parents look like in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: Usually dinner a few nights a week, random kitchen conversations, and weekend chores. My dad and I might do yard stuff Saturday morning, and my mom will ask me about job applications when I am trying to sneak coffee.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating at all?
follow_ups.response: Not seriously. I have gone on dates through friends or Instagram, but I am not in a committed relationship.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family do you go to first when stressed?
follow_ups.response: My mom if it is practical or emotional. My dad if I need a calm reality check and do not want a huge conversation.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Immediate family is really my mom, dad, and younger sister. I have grandparents in California too, but we mostly see them around holidays or family meals.

follow_ups.question: Are you close with your grandparents?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I call my grandmother every couple weeks, and she asks if I have a 'real job' yet, but in a loving way.

follow_ups.question: Any siblings besides Emily?
follow_ups.response: No, just Emily and me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are a huge part of my life. Mateo is probably my closest friend; we play volleyball, hike, and he is the person who will tell me when I am overthinking. I have friends from the SLO beach volleyball club, especially people I see on weekends, and the improv troupe at the SLO Community Center is another circle. There is also a trail crew I hike with in the Santa Lucia foothills, and those people are more outdoorsy and low-drama. I like having different groups because one night can be jokes and improv games, and another morning can be packing trail snacks and getting outside before it gets too hot.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see these friends?
follow_ups.response: Volleyball people about once or twice a week when weather is good, improv usually once a week, and hikes maybe two Saturdays a month.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually hang out?
follow_ups.response: Beaches near San Luis Obispo, coffee shops, somebody's backyard, or downtown Paso if there is live music or a food truck event.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Paso Robles, in a pretty residential area where you can tell families have been there a while. It is not fancy like some of the winery estates, but it is comfortable: single-family homes, pickup trucks, landscaping that gets dry in summer, and people who wave if they recognize you. You are close enough to downtown and tasting rooms that tourism is part of the background, but daily life is still grocery runs, school traffic, and hot afternoons. I like that there are farmers markets, local events, and trails within driving distance. The downside is you really need a car, and rent or housing costs feel way higher than what young people working entry-level jobs can handle.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by name and more by face. My parents know them better than I do, but I will help carry something or chat if we are both outside.

follow_ups.question: What places do you visit most near home?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, the farmers market when I can, local coffee spots, parks, and then I drive toward SLO or the coast for volleyball and hikes.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. I lock my car and do normal common-sense stuff, but I do not feel worried walking around during the day or coming home at night.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that made you feel unsafe?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins or people talking about packages getting taken. Nothing violent that directly affected us.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents feel the same way?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though my mom is more alert about locking doors and making sure my sister texts when she is out.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community, weather, wine country, and access to the coast and trails. The downside is cost, summer heat, needing to drive everywhere, and sometimes feeling like career options are either tourism, agriculture, or leaving.

follow_ups.question: Do you imagine staying in Paso Robles?
follow_ups.response: For the next few years, yes. Long term, maybe I split time between here and somewhere closer to the coast.

follow_ups.question: What would you change about the area?
follow_ups.response: More affordable rentals and better transit between Paso, SLO, and the beach towns.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom, my dad, and my younger sister Emily. My parents own the house, and I have my room from high school, although I have tried to make it feel less like I am still sixteen. My sister has school and activities, so the house is busy in the mornings. We do not have anyone temporary living with us. I help with groceries, cooking sometimes, yard work, driving Emily, and some bills when I have money from event gigs or savings.

follow_ups.question: What household chore is mostly yours?
follow_ups.response: I do a lot of grocery runs, dishes after dinner, and grilling when we cook outside. Yard cleanup also lands on me and my dad.

follow_ups.question: Do you have enough privacy at home?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, but it is still living with family. If I am on a job call or editing photos, I usually close my door and hope nobody knocks.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent member of the household.

follow_ups.question: No one staying for work or school temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No, nobody like that.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been stable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes a cousin or grandparent stays one night around holidays, but not regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Do friends stay over?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. My friends usually head home after hanging out.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week is uneven because I am not in a regular job right now. On weekdays I usually wake up around 7:30 or 8:00, make coffee, check messages, and try to spend part of the morning applying for hospitality or social media roles. Some days I help at the community garden or do errands for my family. Afternoons might be Lightroom editing, working on a social post idea for a friend, or taking my sister somewhere. Evenings are when I have improv practice, volleyball, or meet friends. Weekends are more active: beach volleyball in SLO, hikes, farmers market, winery events, or family chores.

follow_ups.question: What is the most structured day of your week?
follow_ups.response: Improv practice night, because it starts at a set time at the SLO Community Center and I have to plan the drive.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 11:30, unless I drink coffee too late or get stuck editing photos.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: At the moment I am not formally employed. I used to work part time at a local cafe, mostly mornings and weekend shifts, doing register, drinks, cleaning, and customer service. Over the past year I have picked up informal event help here and there, like check-in tables, setup, photos, or social posts for small local events, but not a steady payroll job. I am applying for winery event assistant jobs and social media coordinator roles. I would like something with weekends sometimes because that is when tourism happens, but I also want enough structure that I can learn the business side.

follow_ups.question: Why did the cafe job end?
follow_ups.response: The schedule changed and I wanted to focus on school and hospitality applications. It was not dramatic; I left on decent terms.

follow_ups.question: What kind of job posting gets your attention?
follow_ups.response: Anything that combines guest experience, events, tasting room support, and social media content, especially if they mention sustainability or local partnerships.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help around the house more than I probably admit to friends. I drive my sister when my parents are working, do grocery runs, cook dinner once or twice a week, and help my dad with outdoor chores. I also volunteer at the community garden, usually one morning or afternoon a week, depending on the season. For myself, I try to keep volleyball and hiking on the calendar because if I do not schedule active stuff, I get restless and spend too much time scrolling.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually cook for the family?
follow_ups.response: Grilled salmon, tomato salad, pasta with vegetables, or risotto if I have time and patience.

follow_ups.question: What responsibility do you put off the most?
follow_ups.response: Paperwork and applications. I can plan a whole event faster than I can finish one boring online form.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is not having the cafe schedule anchoring my week. At first that felt freeing, but then I realized I needed to create my own structure or the days got blurry. I started making a loose Monday morning plan: applications, workouts, volunteering, and one networking message. I have also been drinking less afternoon coffee because it was making me jittery and messing with sleep. My routine feels like a work in progress.

follow_ups.question: What helped you add structure?
follow_ups.response: Using Google Calendar and setting small tasks instead of writing one giant goal like 'get career together.'

follow_ups.question: What still throws the routine off?
follow_ups.response: Last-minute plans with friends or overcommitting to help with events because I do not want to miss opportunities.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so this does not apply to me. The closest thing is sometimes helping my younger sister with rides during the school year.

follow_ups.question: Do child care responsibilities affect your schedule at all?
follow_ups.response: No, not child care. Family rides can affect it, but it is manageable.

follow_ups.question: Do you want children someday?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, but not anytime soon. I want to be financially stable first.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have been pretty limited. I have been pulled over once for speeding on the highway between Paso and SLO, and I got a warning because I was only a little over and was polite. I have seen police at downtown events and festivals, mostly doing traffic or crowd control. I do not have a personal history of being targeted or anything like that, but I know that is not everyone's experience. Growing up here, I mostly thought of law enforcement as part of the background of public events.

follow_ups.question: How did the traffic stop feel?
follow_ups.response: Nerve-racking in the normal way, but not scary. I kept my hands visible and just answered questions.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers personally?
follow_ups.response: No, not personally, though my parents know a few people through community connections.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing them at big events, like wine festivals, parades, and busy downtown nights. I also remember school presentations about safe driving and drinking, which felt repetitive but probably useful.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever been involved at an event you helped with?
follow_ups.response: Only for permits, traffic flow, or making sure people did not park badly. Nothing serious.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends talk about police much?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially around protests or national news, but not every day.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has either. I know a friend of a friend who got a DUI, and that made people in my circle more serious about designated drivers after tasting events.

follow_ups.question: Did that change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: Yes. If wine tasting is involved, we plan rides or someone stays sober.

follow_ups.question: Was that person close to you?
follow_ups.response: Not close, but close enough that it felt real instead of just a warning story.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote, but I am still building the habit. I voted in the 2024 presidential election and paid more attention than I did when I first turned eighteen. Local elections are harder for me because there are school board, water, housing, and county issues where I have to do more homework. I usually use the voter guide and ask people I trust, but I try not to just copy my parents. I care about local decisions because tourism, housing, and environment all affect whether someone my age can actually stay here.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: By mail. I like having time to look things up instead of guessing at a polling place.

follow_ups.question: What local issue gets your attention most?
follow_ups.response: Housing affordability, because a lot of young people working in hospitality cannot afford to live near the jobs.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left, practical, and probably more local-issue focused than ideological. I care about climate, water use, housing, and making sure people who work in service jobs can afford basic life. At the same time, I grew up around small business owners, agriculture, and wineries, so I do not think every regulation is automatically good just because it sounds nice. I want environmental rules that actually work and do not just crush smaller local operations while bigger companies adapt easily. On social issues I am pretty open and live-and-let-live; most of my friends are mixed politically but generally accepting. I do not like politics when it turns into people performing online instead of solving things. I trust local community action more than national shouting, though national politics obviously matters.

follow_ups.question: What shaped that center-left view?
follow_ups.response: Growing up in a place where the environment and economy are tied together. If the land, water, and community get damaged, the whole local identity gets damaged too.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents share your politics?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. My mom is more moderate Democrat, and my dad is more independent and business-minded, so dinner conversations can get interesting.

follow_ups.question: What political issue feels most personal?
follow_ups.response: Affordable housing and water use. Those are not abstract here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more interested in local government than I used to be. When I was younger, politics meant presidents, arguments, and people reposting stuff. Now I see that county decisions about housing, water, tourism permits, roads, and environmental rules shape daily life. I also became more serious about climate issues after hiking areas affected by drought and seeing how hot summers have felt. I am still not the person reading every council agenda, but I pay more attention than before.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific local decision that caught your attention?
follow_ups.response: Conversations about short-term rentals and housing availability. It made me realize tourism can help the area and also squeeze locals.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever attended a public meeting?
follow_ups.response: Not yet. I have watched clips online, but attending one is on my list.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say it affected me somewhat. As a white guy in a mostly comfortable Central Coast environment, I know my daily experiences with police and public spaces are not the same as everyone else's. The Black Lives Matter conversations made me more aware of that gap, especially listening to classmates and people online talk about things I had not personally dealt with. It did not become the center of my life every day, but it changed how casually I talk about policing and race. I try to listen more before assuming.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone close to you influence how you thought about it?
follow_ups.response: A couple friends from community college did. They were more direct about experiences with being watched in stores or pulled over, and that stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Did you read or watch anything that changed your view?
follow_ups.response: Mostly interviews, local panels, and journalism shared by people I trust. I am more likely to watch a thoughtful conversation than read a huge policy paper.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issues are real: accountability, unequal treatment, and whether communities feel protected or watched. I also think people get stuck arguing over slogans instead of talking about specific policy changes. I am not an expert, but body cameras, better training, mental health response, and transparency around complaints seem reasonable to me. I try to avoid acting like posting one square or one article means I have done something meaningful. For me, it is more about staying aware and supporting local leaders who take fairness seriously.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. My dad wants specifics before he agrees with anything, and my mom is more emotionally open to the movement's concerns.

follow_ups.question: What do you think people your age get right or wrong about it?
follow_ups.response: We are good at noticing unfairness, but sometimes we move too fast into labeling people instead of persuading them.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think about race as something I used to treat as mostly historical or somewhere else, and now I understand it is present in everyday systems. At the same time, where I live can make it easy to avoid thinking about it deeply because my immediate circle is not always very diverse. I have tried to notice who gets represented at events, whose businesses get promoted, and whether tourism tells the whole story of a region or just the polished version. I do not think guilt by itself is useful, but awareness should lead to different choices.

follow_ups.question: How does that show up in hospitality or tourism?
follow_ups.response: Tourism can flatten a place into wine, food, and scenery. I think good hospitality should include local workers, different communities, and history, not just pretty vineyard photos.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable talking about race?
follow_ups.response: More than before, but I still worry about saying something clumsy. I would rather be corrected than pretend I know everything.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, shared some resources online, and paid more attention to local candidates' views. I have not been a regular protest person, though I did attend one peaceful gathering in SLO with friends.

follow_ups.question: What was that gathering like?
follow_ups.response: Pretty calm and reflective. People had signs, there were speakers, and I mostly listened.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it often?
follow_ups.response: No. I post occasionally, but I try not to make serious issues into personal branding.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends are mixed. Some are very vocal and see racial justice as a major part of their politics. Others agree racism exists but get uncomfortable with activist language or arguments about policing. My family talks about it in a more cautious way, especially my dad, who wants to separate good officers from bad systems. I think most people close to me have at least become more aware, even if they do not all use the same language.

follow_ups.question: Has it caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: A little, usually around social media posts or national news. In person, people are calmer.

follow_ups.question: Who is most vocal in your circle?
follow_ups.response: Friends from community college and improv. Theater people are usually more openly political.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I am active with beach volleyball, hiking, and general outdoor stuff, so I am in decent shape. I do get caffeine jitters when I overdo coffee, and I have had some ankle soreness from volleyball, but nothing major. My sleep is the thing that needs work because if my routine is loose, I stay up late editing photos or scrolling. Mentally, I am usually upbeat, but uncertainty about work can make me anxious.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any diagnosed chronic condition?
follow_ups.response: No diagnosed chronic condition.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually three to five times a week if you count volleyball, hikes, and gym-style workouts at home.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when health is social, like volleyball, hiking, or cooking with fresh produce from the farmers market. It is hard when I am stressed or unstructured because then I drink too much coffee, snack randomly, and stay up late. Living near outdoor places helps a lot. Money can be a factor too because healthy food and gym memberships are not cheap, but I can work around it with home cooking.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meal do you make most?
follow_ups.response: Tomato and mozzarella salad with olives, grilled vegetables, or salmon if it is in the budget.

follow_ups.question: What unhealthy habit shows up first under stress?
follow_ups.response: Too much coffee and procrastinating until I feel more stressed.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I rolled my ankle playing beach volleyball last year, and it bothered me for a few weeks, but it was not broken. I rested, iced it, and wore a brace when I started playing again. I also had a stretch where caffeine and stress made me feel shaky, especially during job application weeks, so I cut back from several coffees to one or two. No major diagnoses, no hospital stays, and no serious injuries.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: No, I went to urgent care only if it got worse, but it improved with rest and a brace.

follow_ups.question: Are the jitters still happening?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but less now that I avoid late coffee and actually eat breakfast.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously blocked me from working or taking care of responsibilities. Minor ankle pain slowed down volleyball and hiking, and stress can make me procrastinate, but I can function.

follow_ups.question: Has anxiety ever stopped you from applying for jobs?
follow_ups.response: It has delayed me, yes. I will overthink a cover letter instead of sending it.

follow_ups.question: Do physical issues limit your routines now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Nothing severe in my immediate family right now. My grandparents have the normal older-person stuff like blood pressure, mobility, and appointments, and that affects family planning sometimes. My mom worries about everyone and tends to be the appointment coordinator. I have helped with rides or errands here and there, but I am not a primary caregiver. It does make me aware that family health can change fast.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever help grandparents directly?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, mostly rides, carrying things, or helping with phones and photos.

follow_ups.question: Does family health affect your work plans?
follow_ups.response: Not directly, but staying local partly means I can help if needed.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I am still on my parents' health insurance, which is a big help. I have not had to completely forgo care because of cost, but I have delayed dental cleanings or checkups longer than I should. My family is pretty good at handling necessary care, but we still notice copays and the cost of prescriptions or dental work.

follow_ups.question: Do you use supplements?

transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, especially because I am around wine culture, but I try to keep it moderate. If I am stressed, I am more likely to drink coffee than alcohol, or go play volleyball. follow_ups.question: Any concerns about substance use in your circle?
